Conclusion/s in relation to relevant materials

41. In light of the above information, I am satisfied, on the balance of probabilities, that FFG
    engaged in fraudulent activity, or more specifically, that it was used as a vehicle through which
    fraud was perpetrated against the NDIS by its key personnel.

42. I give significant weight to the complaints submitted to the NDIS Commission in relation to Ms
    Goodwin and Ms Clulow, the NDIA’s SoFM and the sworn statement of Ms Clulow as these
    distinct pieces of evidence all corroborate the same allegation/s of FFG having been involved in
    defrauding the NDIS over a substantial period of time. The evidence presents a uniform and
    egregious account of FFG’s systems being used, or FFG’s key personnel systemically submitting
    false claims for payments against the NDIS plans of NDIS participants.

43. I note FFG has not provided any evidence to negate the fraud alleged above.




                                                 1388
                                                                                                    T71.1
44. I also acknowledge there are criminal proceedings relating to this matter currently in process
    and a verdict has not yet been reached in those proceedings. However, as a national regulator,
    the NDIS Commission is not constrained from performing its statutory function to protect and
    safeguard NDIS participants whilst there is pending court action. This is particularly true in
    circumstances where the NDIS Commission has conducted an independent investigation in
    accordance with the legislation governing its operations (i.e. the NDIS Act and NDIS Rules) and
    determined that regulatory action is needed immediately to address a serious risk (i.e. financial
    abuse of NDIS participants and perpetration of fraud against the NDIS).

45. Another reason why I am not inclined to await the court outcome is that I am satisfied of the
    veracity of the evidence before me, particularly given:

       a.   the evidence consists of, or involved the forensic examination of FFG’s bank statements
            and payments claims submitted by FFG to the NDIA;

       b.   the evidence has been gathered and scrutinised by the agency specifically charged with
            investigating NDIS fraud (i.e. the NDIA) as well as the Australian Federal Police; and

       c.   the allegations against FFG have been made by various individuals and entities who
            have consistently described the same pattern of fraudulent claiming by FFG.

46. I acknowledge FFG has made submissions in relation to the evidence in this matter, and I deal
    with those below.

The submissions of FFG

47. I have considered the submissions made by Mr Monks, on 30 November 2022 and 20 March
    2023.

48. In summary, the submissions of FFG denied the breadth of allegations put forth by the original
    decision-maker, which were that:

            a. FFG was providing support or services to NDIS participants for which it was not
               registered (i.e. specialist disability accommodation);

            b. the NDIS Commissions had received over 30 complaints regarding the safety and
               quality of supports and services provided by FFG;

            c. the NDIS Commission held information that suggested FFG does not support
               individuals to raise complaints they may have directly with FFG, without fear of
               retaliation from FFG of its key personnel;

            d. FFG does not have a complaints management and resolution system in place that
               ensures complaints are welcomed, acknowledged, respected and well-managed;

            e. FFG does not employ workers who hold the relevant qualifications for their role/s;

            f.   FFG had not been acting with respect for individual rights to freedom of expression,
                 self-determination and decision-making in accordance with applicable laws and
                 conventions. The written communications of FFG with NDIS participants (or their
                 family/support persons) included veiled and direct threats, bullying and harassment;




                                              1389
                                                                                                      T71.1
            g. FFG was not acting with integrity, honesty and transparency. FFG had knowingly
               been submitting false claims for payments to the NDIA, with the intention of
               dishonestly causing a loss to a Commonwealth entity; and

            h. FFG had not taken all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to the exploitation
               of people with disability. FFG had been seeking to act as both an NDIS provider for,
               and the authorised person, on behalf of NDIS participants, to engage with the NDIA
               in relation to their support provision/s and funding decisions.

49. I note that FFG provided a significant amount of information (and evidence to varying extents)
    to the original decision-maker to support its position.

50. Further, a key aspect of FFG’s submissions was the assertion that the original decision-maker
    had failed to afford procedural fairness to FFG, and had not properly considered the
    submissions made by FFG when determining to issue the banning order. (Please refer to
    paragraphs 53-62 below, where I consider these submissions in further detail).

51. As already mentioned above, I have adopted a narrow(er) approach to this internal review and
    based my decision upon a more circumscribed amount of material than that relied upon by the
    original decision-maker, that is, I rely specifically upon the fraud that FFG is alleged to have
    been involved in. Therefore, in my view, it is not necessary or conducive to go into a detailed
    examination of all of the submissions FFG previously made, rather I propose to deal solely with
    the aspects of FFG’s submissions that relate to the matters upon which I have formed my
    decision (given the remaining matters have fallen away). Before, proceeding to do so, however,
    I acknowledge that there were deficiencies and failings by the original decision-maker with
    respect to:

            a. sufficiently providing FFG with information about some of the allegations raised
               against it (noting that FGG was, on balance, adequately informed of the material
               before the original decision-maker); and

            b. clearly communicating his view or analysis of FFG’s submissions. I have reviewed
               internal working documents of the NDIS Commission that demonstrate the original
               decision-maker did consider the submissions of FFG, however, he was not
               persuaded by them. Unfortunately, the original decision failed to clearly articulate
               the reason/s for giving minimal weight to FFG’s submissions.

52. The submissions made by Mr Monks that relate to the issue of fraud are found in paragraph 6
    and on page 11 of the 30 November 2022 submission, and paragraphs 6-7, 16-17, 19-21 and 23-
    24 of the 20 March 2022 submission.

53. In summary, those submissions were that:

       a.   FFG emphatically denies the allegation that false claims were submitted for payment to
            the NDIA with the intention of dishonestly causing a loss to a Commonwealth entity;

       b.   the matter is currently the subject of criminal proceedings and it is inappropriate for
            the NDIS Commission to pursue the allegations until the criminal proceedings have
            been determined;




                                             1390
                                                                                                        T71.1
        c.   in the interests of ‘procedural and substantive justice’, FFG’s ‘fitness to hold an NDIS
             registration’ should not be decided until the criminal proceedings are determined;

        d.   requesting FFG to provide a response in relation to the alleged fraud is inappropriate
             and comprises FFG’s legal defence;

        e.   the NDIS Commission’s issuance of a banning order to FFG indicates that it has pre-
             determined FFG is guilty of the alleged fraud although the relevant evidence has not
             been tested in court yet;

        f.   FFG is concerned by the linkage of, the banning order made against it, to the criminal
             proceedings against Mrs Reid, because in the event that Mrs Reid is found not guilty,
             the banning order would remain in place and unjustifiably penalise FFG after the
             conclusion of the court matter;

        g.   In light of the above paragraph, it would have been prudent for the NDIS Commission
             to maintain the suspension of FFG, rather than issue a banning order to it. Adopting this
             approach would have protected the interests of all parties, including NDIS participants.

        h.   The NDIS Commission has not followed its own Compliance and Enforcement Policy by
             issuing the banning order as there were other regulatory actions available to the NDIS
             Commission to implement, such as the suspension of FFG’s registration.

        i.   The NDIS Commission did not afford FFG procedural fairness (in line with the National
             Disability Insurance Scheme (Procedural Fairness) Guidelines 2018) given it failed to
             provide FFG with a fair opportunity to respond to all allegations against it.

        j.   FFG provided names of witnesses who could support its position in relation to the
             allegations against it. The NDIS Commission did not follow up those witnesses.

54. I consider each of these submissions in turn below.

55. In relation to the submission made by FFG at paragraph 53(a) above, I attributed minimal
    weight to FFG’s categorical denial of the alleged fraud given FFG has not provided any evidence
    to support or exonerate it.

56. In relation to the submissions made by FFG at paragraphs 53(b), (c) and (d) above, I gave
    significant weight to these submissions as I acknowledge that the allegations against Mrs Reid
    (which implicate FFG) have not been proven to the criminal standard. I also acknowledge and
    respect the presumption of innocence in favour of Mrs Reid in relation to the criminal charges.
    However, the submissions of FFG ultimately did not dissuade me from my view that a banning
    order should be made against FFG. As noted earlier, pending court action does not prevent the
    NDIS Commission (or any national regulator) from performing its statutory function/s in the
    interim. Rather, it will often be the case that a regulatory body will need to take action for
    protective purposes until any associated court process is finalised, particularly in circumstances,
    such as the present, where there may be a serious risk involved in the alleged wrongdoing
    remaining unaddressed. I consider there would be a significant and indefensible risk associated
    with FFG being allowed to continue to engage in the NDIS sector until the criminal proceedings
    are determined - the likelihood of further harm to other NDIS participants to whom FFG may




                                               1391
                                                                                                     T71.1
    provide supports or services (i.e. depletion of their NDIS funding) warrants the NDIS
    Commission imposing a banning order at this time to safeguard NDIS participants.

57. In relation to the submissions made by FFG at paragraph 53(e), I gave considerable weight to
    this assertion. I appreciate that, in the context of criminal proceedings, the standard of proof
    that applies is that allegations must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. I am not purporting
    to stand in the shoes of the court or perform its judicial task. The making of a banning order is
    an administrative decision, and it only requires that I be satisfied on the balance of probabilities
    that FFG has engaged in the conduct alleged, which, I am, given the strength of the evidence
    referred to above at paragraphs 41 to 45.

58. In relation to the submission made by FFG at paragraph 53(f) above, I attributed minimal
    weight to FFG’s concerns as it seems the entity does not fully understand the legislative
    framework concerning the issuance of a banning order. In the event that the criminal
    proceedings determine Mrs Reid is not guilty of the alleged fraud, section 73ZO of the NDIS Act
    enables the NDIS Commissioner to vary or revoke the banning order against FFG if satisfied that
    it is appropriate to do so. Further, a variation or revocation can be effected on the
    Commissioner’s own initiative or upon application by FFG.

59. In relation to the submission made by FFG at paragraphs 53(g) and (h) above, I have given these
    submissions minimal weight as they, similarly, indicate that FFG does not fully understand the
    legislative provisions regarding the use of suspensions under section 73N of the NDIS Act.
    Firstly, if the NDIS commission were to suspend the registration of FFG instead of making a
    banning order against FFG, it would not provide a sufficient level of safeguarding to NDIS
    participants. A suspension would only prohibit FFG from providing supports and services for
    which it must be registered to deliver to NDIS participants. Meaning, FFG could continue to
    operate as an unregistered NDIS provider. Secondly, the particular use of the suspension power
    that is contended for by FFG is not appropriate. A suspension under section 73N is designed to
    be a temporary action (only in effect for 30 days) to address immediate or significant concerns
    held in relation to an NDIS provider. It is not intended to be used repeatedly or for a substantial
    period of time in relation to the same NDIS provider. If a suspension were to be consecutively
    issued, it would signal that a more permanent or enduring form of regulatory action is, in fact,
    needed.

60. In relation to the submission made by FFG at paragraph 53(i) above, I gave significant weight to
    FFG’s concerns. As noted above, there were some procedural failings or deficiencies associated
    with the original decision, which I have given close attention to. To that end, on 1 June 2023, I
    notified FFG of the decision I was proposing to making on internal review and provided FFG
    with a copy of the material(s) I had relied upon in forming my preliminary view (i.e. the sworn
    statements of Ms Goodwin and Ms Clulow, the NDIA SoFM and a summary of the complaints
    submitted to the NDIS Commission in relation to Ms Goodwin and Ms Clulow). Further, I invited
    FFG to make submissions to me in relation to that information and the proposed internal
    review decision.

    Most importantly, the matters (or allegations) in relation to which FFG alleges that the original
    decision-maker failed to observe procedural fairness, notably, do not form part of my decision.
    I have based my decision on distinct considerations – i.e. the alleged fraud against the NDIS –




                                               1392
                                                                                                   T71.1
    which I have ensured FFG has been sufficiently informed of, and given a fair opportunity to
    respond to.

61. In relation to the submission made by FFG at paragraph 53(j) above, I have attributed no weight
    to the assertion that the NDIS Commission failed to follow up with witnesses whom FFG
    identified as being able to support FFG’s position. I can find no evidence of FFG having provided
    the original decision-maker (or I) with the names or contact details of relevant witnesses. I note
    that, in the context of a separate but related matter, namely the decision to issue a banning
    order to Mr Reid, Mr Monk claimed to be in possession of evidence that exculpated Mr Reid of
    the wrongdoing he was alleged to have engaged in, but he did not provide such information
    (even when requested to do so by the original decision-maker).

Section 73ZN(1)(a) of the NDIS Act – power to issue a banning order where the registration of a
registered NDIS provider has been revoked

62. The banning order issued to FFG was made pursuant to section 73ZN(1)(a) of the NDIS Act.

63. The statutory test for issuing a banning order under this provision is singular. The NDIS
    Commissioner (or her delegate) must have revoked the registration of a person as a registered
    NDIS provider. Provided that process of revocation had occurred, it was open to the original
    decision-maker to impose a banning order.

64. I have been provided with a copy of the decision to revoke the registration of FFG on 20
    December 2022. I am, therefore, satisfied that it was open to the original decision-maker to
    issue a banning order to FFG.

65. However, as mentioned above (at paragraphs 36-37) the original decision-maker should have
    clearly articulated the reason(s) as to why a banning order was warranted in the circumstances.
    The mere fact that section 73ZN(1)(a) conferred upon the original decision-maker the power to
    use this statutory tool, did not suffice or justify the use of it.

66. Despite the original decision-maker’s omission in this regard, in my view there are compelling
    reasons to support or warrant the issuance of a banning order to FFG. Those reasons are that:

        a.   FFG was, in effect, used by the key personnel of the company as a vehicle to perpetrate
             the alleged fraud against the NDIS. In my view, where an entity has facilitated the
             commission of fraud, it is not appropriate for it to remain engaged in the NDIS sector
             given the serious risk it poses to NDIS participants (i.e. the depletion of their NDIS
             funding);

        b.   The revocation of FFG’s registration does not provide a complete or wholesale level of
             safeguarding to NDIS participants given that FFG remains capable of providing supports
             and services to NDIS participants for which registration is not a requirement. The
             classes of supports and services that can be delivered by an unregistered NDIS provider
             are vast and would enable FFG to have access to the NDIS plans of thousands of NDIS
             participants.

        c.   I acknowledge the making of a banning order in respect of FFG will significantly impact
             the operations of the business, and I have taken this into account. However, I consider




                                              1393
                                                                                                    T71.1
             that the competing interest of ensuring NDIS participants, who may not be able to fully
             protect their own interests and who have a statutory right to safe services and
             protection from violence, abuse and exploitation, is paramount and takes precedence
             over the detriment FFG may experience if banned.

67. Further, I agree with the reasoning expressed by the original decision-maker in paragraphs 27 –
    33 of the original decision in so far that he explained the objects of the NDIS Act (contained in
    section 3) as well as section 4(17)(b) of the NDIS Act are factors which also support the
    imposition of a banning order against FFG.

68. Therefore, I am satisfied that the making of a banning order against FFG is the correct and
    preferable decision in the circumstances.

The NDIS Commission Banning Order Policy

69. The NDIS Commission Banning Order Policy contemplates that a banning order can be ‘issued
    pending the determination of [criminal] charges’ if, in the circumstances, the information and
    evidence obtained by the NDIS Commission supports a view that a banning order is warranted
    and appropriate.

70. For the reasons already noted above (at paragraphs 41 and 45), I consider a banning order
    against FFG to be warranted and appropriate.

Requirement to take proportionate and risk responsive action under NDIS Act

71. The NDIS Commission is required to conduct compliance and enforcement activities in a risk
    responsive and proportionate manner (per section 181D(4)(b) of the NDIS Act).

72. The NDIS Commission’s Banning Order Policy notes that a banning order can have a significant
    impact on the recipient and on people with disability, and as such, it will be reserved for
    circumstances where it is needed to protect people with disability from the risk of being
    exposed to conduct that falls well short of acceptable standards. However, a banning order
    should not be for a longer period than is considered necessary.

73. Having regard to the criminal proceedings pending against Mrs Reid (which, as noted above,
    implicate FFG in fraudulent activity), I consider that a banning order for a period of 3 years is a
    risk responsive and proportionate measure as it corresponds with the amount of time it is
    reasonably expected to take for the criminal proceedings to be finally determined by the court.
    Upon determination of those proceedings, the banning order against FFG can be revisited and
    consideration given to whether it should be varied any further (or revoked entirely). I note a
    variation or revocation of the banning order could also take place prior to the determination of
    the court proceedings if appropriate or necessary.

74. In the meantime, the banning order will protect NDIS participants from the risk of having
    fraudulent claims submitted against their NDIS plans and their funding for disability supports or
    services being depleted.

75. The banning order will, therefore, remain in place until 12:00am on 21 December 2025
    (AWST).

   76. The NDIS Provider Register published on the NDIS Commission’s website will be updated to
       reflect the banning order made against FFG was affirmed on internal review.

The decision
I have made a decision to revoke the registration of Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd, commencing
from the date of this notice. Reasons for my decision are outlined in Attachment A.

I have revoked the registration of the Provider because I reasonably believe that the Provider has
contravened, is contravening, or is proposing to contravene the NDIS Act, as provided for by section
73P(1)(a) of the NDIS Act. Section 73ZN(8)(b) of the NDIS Act also gives me the power to make a
Banning Order if I have revoked the registration as an NDIS provider. Please refer to the separate
letter dated 20 December 2022 regarding the Banning Order.

Non-compliance with the revocation

contravention of section 73B of the NDIS Act, insofar as the NDIS rules may require that specified
classes of supports provided under a participant’s plans be provided only by NDIS providers who are
registered to provide those classes of supports. A contravention of section 73B attract a civil penalty
up to $55,500 for individuals.

which must include certain information for each person who is a registered NDIS provider. Relevant
to this matter, section 73ZS(5)(e) permits the NDIS Provider Register to include information about a

Submissions

21. The Commission received a submission on 30 November 2022 (the extended submission date).

    provide the Commission with additional evidence to support your position.

27. As part of my considerations I am obliged to consider the NDIS Act. Section 3 of the NDIS Act
    contains the objects of the NDIS Act, which includes:

            a. Supporting the independence and social and economic participation of people with
               disability.

            b. Enabling people with disability to exercise choice and control in the pursuit of their
               goals and the panning and delivery of their supports.

                                               1401

            c. Protecting and preventing people with disability from experiencing harm arising
               from poor quality or unsafe supports or services provided under the National
               Disability Insurance Scheme.

28. In giving effect to the objects of the NDIS Act, including those outlined above, section 3(3)(b)
    requires regard to be had to the need to ensure financial sustainability of the National Disability
    Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Similarly, as set out in NDIS Act section 4(17) it is the intention of the
    Parliament that the Commissioner, amongst others, have regard to the need to ensure financial
    sustainability of the NDIS in performing functions and exercising powers under the NDIS Act.

29. As a registered NDIS provider, Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd, elected to participate in a
    national scheme aimed at assisting those who have permanent and significant disability, and
    providing those participants with choice and control over their supports and services, and their
    selection of the providers of those supports and services.

30. My view is that the need to protect the interests of people with disability, who may be
    particularly vulnerable, and ensure they are kept safe, outweighs the Provider’s interest in
    continuing to provide supports or services to people with disability.

31. The matters set out above demonstrates conduct that falls well below the standard and quality
    of care expected from NDIS providers when providing supports or services to people with
    disability.

32. The information before me in relation to the protracted length of time over which this conduct
    took place and continued as well as the instances of similar misconduct against multiple NDIS
    participants suggests that Provider’s conduct was systemic in nature.

33. I am also of the view that allowing the Provider to continue providing supports or services to
    people with disability would jeopardise public trust in the NDIS.

34. I consider the alleged conduct of the Provider is entirely relevant to my assessment of the
    Provider’s suitability to be involved in the provision of supports or services to NDIS participants,
    in considering the objects and principles of the NDIS Act. This is particularly the case as the
    parties impacted by the Provider’s actions are NDIS participants.

35. Having weighed all the evidence at hand I reasonably believe that the Provider, has contravened,
    is contravening, or is proposing to contravene, the Act.

36. I am therefore satisfied that the power to revoke the registration is available to me and that it is,
    in all of the circumstances, a risk responsive and proportionate response.

                     NATIONAL DISABILITY INSURANCE SCHEME ACT 2013 (Cth)
                                        SECTION 73ZN
                                       BANNING ORDER

I, Philip Halton, give this Banning Order to Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd on the basis that, I have
revoked the registration of the person as a registered NDIS provider. (NDIS Act s73ZN(1)(a)).

Pursuant to section 73ZN(1)(a) of the NDIS Act, I prohibit Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd from
providing supports and services, directly or indirectly, to NDIS-funded participants for a period of ten
(10) years from the date that this order takes effect.

My reasons for making this order are set out in the enclosed statement of reasons.

This order takes effect on Tuesday, 20 December 2022 at 5:30pm (AWST).

                    NATIONAL DISABILITY INSURANCE SCHEME ACT 2013 (Cth)
                    SECTION 73ZN BANNING ORDER- STATEMENT OF REASONS

This is a statement of reasons for the making of a Banning Order on 20 December 2022 against
Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd, under section 73ZN of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act
2013 (NDIS Act).
Procedural steps
I refer to my letter dated 19 October 2022 advising of the proposed revocation of the registration of
Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd ACN 643 878 639 (“the Provider”) and the relevant facts and matters
that I have considered in reaching the view the Provider has contravened, is contravening, or is likely
to contravene the NDIS Act.
I also gave the Provider the opportunity to make submissions about this due no later than 5.00pm
(AWST) on 16 November 2022.
I received a request for an extension to that timeframe and granted additional time for submissions
through to 30 November 2022 (the extended submission date).

I acknowledge the submission sent by Mr Tom Monks, Principal Director, Tom & Co Legal Pty Ltd to
the Commission on 30 November 2022. The Commission has carefully considered the contents of
the submission to determine whether to revoke the registration of the Provider.

As detailed in a letter of 20 December 2022, I have made a decision to revoke the registration of the
Provider, commencing from the date of the notice.

As I have revoked the registration of the Provider, I have made the decision to make a Banning Order
against the Provider, as provided for by section 73ZN(1)(a) of the NDIS Act.

The relevant facts and information held by the Commission in forming the view to revoke the
registration and make a Banning Order against the Provider are set out below.

Relevant facts and information

1. Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd is a registered NDIS provider, registration 4-4GHG-1073.
2. Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd (the Provider) is registered to provide the following services:
          Item 8 – Assistance with travel/transport arrangements; and
          Item 20 – Household tasks.

3. It is alleged that the Provider is providing supports to participants that the provider is not
   registered to provide. The Forward Focused Group website (www.forwardfocusedgroup.com.au)
   in its ‘Service Offerings’ offered SDA (Specialist Disability Accommodation) at three suburb
   locations. The Forward Focused Group Facebook page posted on at least two occasions 18 July
   2022 and 28 September 2022 with the SDA service offering.
4. Since September 2021, the Commission has received over 30 complaints regarding the safety
   and quality of supports provided by Forward Focused Group. The Commission also holds
   information that suggests that the Provider does not support individuals to raise any complaints
   they may have directly with the provider, without fear of retaliation from the Provider or the key
   personnel.



                                  NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                    Page 4 of 8
                                               1406
                                                                                             ATTACHMENT B

                                                                                                             T73


5. This information strongly indicates that the Provider does not have a complaints management
    and resolution system in place that ensures that complaints are welcomed, acknowledged,
    respected and well-managed.
6. The Commission holds information that the Provider does not employ workers who hold the
    relevant qualifications for their roles. The FFG website (www.forwardfocusedgroup.com.au) in
    its ‘Our Team’ section stated that Ms Sally See was employed by Forward Focused Group as a
    Counsellor. Ms See does not hold qualifications with either the Australian Counselling
    Association (www.theaca.net.au) or with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency
    (www.ahpra.gov.au). The Commission does not hold any records of contact information or
    worker screening conducted for Ms See.
7. The Commission holds information that the Provider is not acting with respect for individual
    rights to freedom of expression, self-determination and decision-making in accordance with
    applicable laws and conventions. Across June and July 2022, participants including Corina
    Abraham, Sarah-Jane Clulow, and Alexsis Bott all sought to amend or cease service agreements
    with the Provider. The written email engagement with the Provider indicated non-compliance
    with the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Code of Conduct) Rules 2018 and included both
    veiled and direct threats, bullying and harassment. By way of example,
    a. Across May and June 2022, the Provider attempted to obtain control of participant funds
         and participants supports for participant Alexsis Bott. When the participant confirmed, in
         writing that they didn’t want to take the action to release their funds from the existing
         manager the Founding Executive Director writes “we will be terminating your services with
         us effective immediately”.
    b. Series of emails 24 June 2022 to 19 June 2022 regarding participant Sarah-Jane Clulow
         advising a four week notice for service termination. The emails show that the participant
         was seeking review of an invoice for services not received.
    c. On 1 July 2022, the Provider responds to an account statement from a supplier stating that,
         “we will no longer pay any invoices for Sarah. She has terminated her contract with us.”
    d. Series of emails 15 June 2022 to 19 June 2022 regarding participant Corina Abraham ceasing
         some services with Hybrid Hive. The participant seeks to meet to discuss their concerns. By
         email dated 19 June, the Provider through Vida Reid purports to cease support coordination
         and terminate the contract for all services with immediate effect. The email claims “ongoing
         abusive manner of our staff by yourself and the break in trust” as the grounds. The email
         includes a perceived threat that invoices are to be paid immediately or be reported to the
         NDIS.
    e. Email 16 June 2022 by the Founding Director to participant, Ms Abraham, provides that the
         support worker has a non-compete and non-disclosure contract which will prevent her for
         working privately for the participant. It also states that if the participant had “come to us in
         good faith…I would have said okay.”
    f. Email 16 June 2022 by the Founding Director to participant, Ms Abraham, “I would like all of
         your outstanding invoices paid immediately please or I will report this to the NDIS”.
8. The Commission holds information that the Provider is not acting with integrity, honesty and
    transparency.
9. It is alleged that Forward Focused Group knowingly submitted false claims for payments to the
    National Disability Insurance Scheme (Scheme), with the intention of dishonestly causing a loss
    to another person, namely the NDIA, a Commonwealth entity. The Commission is aware of
    questions about invoices raised against multiple participants.
10. The Commission holds information about participants Tiffany Rose and Andrew Hahn on dates
    known between 26 November 2021 and 14 June 2022, which show that the Provider generated


                                   NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                      Page 5 of 8
                                                1407
                                                                                         ATTACHMENT B

                                                                                                         T73


    invoices that did not match the services provided, or were generated without the necessary
    Plans or Services Agreements in place.
11. The Commission also holds information, through emails dated 3 May and 9 May 2022, which
    show that the Founding Executive Director is withholding information from other staff of the
    Provider on potentially fraudulent invoices. By way of example,
    a. Internal email dated 3 May 2022 from former employee to the Chief Financial Officer raising
        questions regarding an invoice for Support Coordination services for participant that
        Forward Focused Group had not provided.
12. The Commission holds records of correspondence between the Provider and participants which
    reflects a lack of integrity and honesty in dealings including accusations of non-payment or
    broken trust as grounds for the Provider to immediately terminate engagements with
    participants. By way of example,
    a. Termination Notice Letter from DFG Legal WA dated 31 March 2022 requesting that
        participant Andrew Hahn vacate a Forward Focused Group-managed property due to
        “serious misconduct” and “failing to pay the fortnightly lodging fee”. The Commission holds
        a record of an email from the advocate of the participant dated 27 March 2022, requesting
        that “unsubstantiated threats of eviction” from the Provider cease.
13. The Commission holds information that the Provider has not taken all reasonable steps to
    prevent and respond to exploitation of people with disability.
14. The Commission holds information that the Provider is seeking to act as both the service
    provider and the authorized person on behalf of a participant to engage with the NDIA in
    relation to support provision and funding decisions. By way of example,
    a. The Commission holds a record of a Forward Focused Group document titled ‘FM Consent
        Third Party to Act’ which provides ongoing consent for any Forward Focused staff member
        (contact Vida Reid), which includes consent to request review of NDIA decisions and manage
        complaints made by participant Meghan Goodwin.
15. The nature of the information held by the Commission strongly suggests to me that the Provider
    has contravened, is contravening, or is proposing to contravene the NDIS Act (as provided for by
    section 73P(1)(a) of the NDIS Act).
16. The NDIS Act s73J requires providers to comply with registration conditions. It is a condition of
    registration that providers comply with the Rules. The National Disability Insurance Scheme
    (Provider Registration and Practice Standards) Rules 2018 (the Practice Standards Rules) section
    7(1) requires providers to be registered to provide Specialist Disability Accommodation (SDA).
17. The Provider is clearly advertising the provision of supports that you are not registered to
    supply.
18. The allegations and information held by the Commission indicate a significant amount of false
    claims against the Scheme, that could have otherwise have been directed to fund essential
    supports and services to people with disability.
19. The Provider’s practice of billing multiple NDIS participants for supports and services not
    provided compromised the integrity of the Scheme and deprived these NDIS participants of
    receiving necessary supports and services that they relied upon and were entitled to receive.
20. The information available to the Commission regarding the way in which the Provider handles
    complaints also suggests that the Provider has failed its obligation under the NDIS Practice
    Standards to implement a complaints management and resolution system that ensures that
    complaints made by all parties are welcomed, acknowledged, respected and well-managed. My
    view, based on the information available to the Commission, is that Provider does not provide a
    supportive environment for any person who makes complaints.

Submissions
21. The Commission received a submission on 30 November 2022 (the extended submission date).
22. Your submission notes that a request for further time and further information were not
    responded to however, the Commission did respond to this request. This is evidenced by the
    Commission’s acceptance of the submission on 30 November 2022 (the extended submission
    date).
23. Your submission responds to a number of facts and information we raised in the notice of
    intention to the provider dated 19 October 2022.
24. Your submission confirms that the Provider held relevant information in relation to the issues
    identified.
25. Your submission denies all allegations.
26. I have carefully considered the information provided in your submissions alongside previous
    information outlined in the letter dated 19 October 2022. I note your submission does not
    provide the Commission with additional evidence to support your position.
27. As part of my considerations I am obliged to consider the NDIS Act. Section 3 of the NDIS Act
    contains the objects of the NDIS Act, which includes:
             a. Supporting the independence and social and economic participation of people with
                 disability.
             b. Enabling people with disability to exercise choice and control in the pursuit of their
                 goals and the panning and delivery of their supports.
             c. Protecting and preventing people with disability from experiencing harm arising
                 from poor quality or unsafe supports or services provided under the National
                 Disability Insurance Scheme.
28. In giving effect to the objects of the NDIS Act, including those outlined above, section 3(3)(b)
    requires regard to be had to the need to ensure financial sustainability of the National Disability
    Insurance Scheme (NDIS). Similarly, as set out in NDIS Act section 4(17) it is the intention of the
    Parliament that the Commissioner, amongst others, have regard to the need to ensure financial
    sustainability of the NDIS in performing functions and exercising powers under the NDIS Act.

29. As a registered NDIS provider, Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd, elected to participate in a
    national scheme aimed at assisting those who have permanent and significant disability, and
    providing those participants with choice and control over their supports and services, and their
    selection of the providers of those supports and services.

30. My view is that the need to protect the interests of people with disability, who may be
    particularly vulnerable, and ensure they are kept safe, outweighs the Provider’s interest in
    continuing to provide supports or services to people with disability.

31. The matters set out above demonstrates conduct that falls well below the standard and quality
    of care expected from NDIS providers when providing supports or services to people with
    disability.
32. The information before me in relation to the protracted length of time over which this conduct
    took place and continued as well as the instances of similar misconduct against multiple NDIS
    participants suggests that Provider’s conduct was systemic in nature.
33. I am also of the view that allowing the Provider to continue providing supports or services to
    people with disability would jeopardise public trust in the NDIS.




                                  NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                     Page 7 of 8
                                               1409
                                                                                            ATTACHMENT B

                                                                                                            T73


34. I consider the alleged conduct of the Provider is entirely relevant to my assessment of the
    Provider’s suitability to be involved in the provision of supports or services to NDIS participants,
    in considering the objects and principles of the NDIS Act. This is particularly the case as the
    parties impacted by the Provider’s actions are NDIS participants.
35. Having weighed all the evidence at hand I reasonably believe that the Provider, has contravened,
    is contravening, or is proposing to contravene, the Act.
36. I am therefore satisfied that the power to revoke the registration is available to me and that it is,
    in all of the circumstances, a risk responsive and proportionate response. I am therefore also
    satisfied that the power to issue a Banning Order is available to me.
37. For the avoidance of doubt, the Banning Order will prevent the Provider from having any
    involvement whether directly or indirectly in the delivery, coordination and management of
    NDIS-funded supports and services to people with disability.
38. I consider that a timeframe of 10 years is appropriate and will provide a strong level of
    protection for people with disability.

As advised in the notices of intention, no decisions have yet been finalised. The Commission will closely
consider all submissions received prior to this new deadline but, consistent with our original notice, will
progress to making final decisions even if submissions are not provided.

In relation to the suspension of registration of Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd (4-4GHG-1073) this
commenced on 19 October 2022 (the date of the Notice). The current suspension is in effect until
19 November 2022. The provisions of the NDIS Act do not provide for submissions to be made upon a
decision to suspend the registration of a provider but, rather, make provision for a review of such a decision
under s.100 of that Act. I understand your client, Ms Reid, has lodged an application for such a review on
Friday 11 November 2022.

If you have questions about this letter, please email WACompliance@ndiscommission.gov.au.

                Notice of Suspension of your provider registration (4-4GHG-1073)
              under section 73N of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013
                                      with immediate effect.


The National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (NDIS Act) gives me, as the Commissioner’s
delegate, the power to suspend the registration of a registered NDIS provider for a specified period,
no longer than thirty (30) days.

I have made the decision to suspend the registration of Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd, registration
number 4-4GHG-1073, for a period of 30 days, commencing from the date of this notice.

I have suspended your registration as a registered NDIS provider because I reasonably believe that
you have contravened sections 73V (the NDIS Code of Conduct), 73B (Requirement to be a
registered NDIS provider) and 73J (compliance with conditions of your registration) of the NDIS Act,
as provided for by section 73N(1)(a) of the NDIS Act.

The suspension means your registration ceases to have effect until 19 November 2022. The reasons
for my decision to suspend your registration are attached to this notice (Annexure A).

NDIS Provider Register

Section 73ZS of the NDIS Act requires the Commissioner to maintain the NDIS Provider Register
which must include certain information for each person who is a registered NDIS provider. This
includes if the registration of a person is suspended, information about the suspension. As I have
decided to suspend your registration with immediate effect, this information will be included on the
NDIS Provider Register, and published online.

Review under section 100 of the NDIS Act

You may request a review of my decision to suspend your registration within 3 months from the
date that the suspension takes effect.

Any application you may make for an internal review would be dealt with by someone other than
me, the original decision-maker.




                                  NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                                1
                                               1417
                                                                                                          T77
Should you wish to request a review of my decision, you may make the request in writing and email
it to review@ndiscommission.gov.au or send it by post, addressed to:

        Branch Head, Operations - North Central West
        NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission
        PO Box 2862
        BRISBANE QLD 4001

Alternatively, you may telephone my office on (07) 3237 6559 to request a review of the decision or
arrange to make the request in person.

Once any review of the decision has been finalised by the reviewer, you may also seek a further
review of the decision by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal as provided for under section 103 of
the NDIS Act.

Non-compliance with the suspension

Please note that engaging in conduct that breaches the suspension of registration may be a
contravention of section 73B of the NDIS Act, insofar as the NDIS rules may require that specified
classes of supports provided under a participant’s plans be provided only by NDIS providers who are
registered to provide those classes of supports. A contravention of section 73B attract a civil penalty
up to $55,500 for individuals.

Reasons for the decision to suspend your registration

Legislative provisions

Section 73J of the NDIS Act provides that registered NDIS providers must comply with conditions of
registration. The conditions they are subject to include those provided at section 73F of the NDIS
Act.

Section 73F of the NDIS Act states that the registration of a person as a registered NDIS provider is
subject to a number of conditions. These conditions include:

    •       Section 73F(2)(b) - a condition that the person comply with all applicable requirements of
            the NDIS Code of Conduct;
    •       Section 73F(2)(c) - a condition that the person comply with all applicable standards and
            other requirements of the NDIS Practice Standards;

Section 73T(1) of the NDIS Act states that the National Disability Insurance Scheme rules may make
provision for or in relation to standards concerning the quality of supports or services to be provided
by registered NDIS providers.

NDIS Code of Conduct

The NDIS Code of Conduct is set out in section 6 of the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Code of
Conduct) Rules 2018 (Code of Conduct Rules). Relevantly, Code-covered persons must, when
providing supports or services to people with disability:

        •      act with respect for individual rights to freedom of expression, self-determination and
               decision-making in accordance with applicable laws and conventions (section 6(a));
        •      act with integrity, honesty and transparency (section 6(d));
        •      take all reasonable steps to prevent and respond to all forms of violence against, and
               exploitation, neglect and abuse of, people with disability (section 6(f)).

Practice Standards

Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd is registered to provide the following classes of supports under the
National Disability Insurance Scheme (Provider Registration and Practice Standards) Rules 2018 (the
Practice Standards Rules):

    •       Item 8 – Assistance with travel/transport arrangements
    •       Item 20 – Household tasks.

In order to remain registered for the above classes of supports, Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd must
comply with the Practice Standards outlined in Schedule 8 of the Practice Standards Rules.

   generated invoices that did not match the services provided, or were generated without the
   necessary Plans or Services Agreements in place.

   The Commission also holds information, through emails dated 3 May and 9 May 2022, which
   show that the Founding Executive Director is withholding information from other staff of the
   Provider on potentially fraudulent invoices. By way of example,

       a. Internal email dated 3 May 2022 from a former employee to the Chief Financial
           Officer raising questions regarding an invoice for Support Coordination services for
           participant that Forward Focused Group had not provided.
   The Commission holds records of correspondence between the Provider and participants
   which reflects a lack of integrity and honesty in dealings including accusations of non-
   payment or broken trust as grounds for the Provider to immediately terminate engagements
   with participants. By way of example,

       a. Termination Notice Letter from DFG Legal WA dated 31 March 2022 requesting that
          participant Andrew Hahn vacate a Forward Focused Group-managed property due
          to “serious misconduct” and “failing to pay the fortnightly lodging fee”. The
          Commission holds a record of an email from the advocate of the participant dated
          27 March 2022, requesting that “unsubstantiated threats of eviction” from the
          Provider cease.

9. The Commission holds information that the Provider has not taken all reasonable steps to
   prevent and respond to exploitation of people with disability.

   The Commission holds information that the Provider is seeking to act as both the service
   provider and the authorized person on behalf of a participant to engage with the NDIA in
   relation to support provision and funding decisions. By way of example,

       a. The Commission holds a record of a Forward Focused Group document titled ‘FM
          Consent Third Party to Act’ which provides ongoing consent for any Forward



                              NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                                 5
                                           1421
                                                                                                      T77
            Focused staff member (contact Vida Reid), which includes consent to request review
            of NDIA decisions and manage complaints made by participant Meghan Goodwin.

Concerns about contraventions of the NDIS Act

1. The nature of the information held by the Commission strongly suggests to me that the
   Provider has contravened, is contravening, or is proposing to contravene the NDIS Act (as
   provided for by section 73P(1)(a) of the NDIS Act).

2. The NDIS Act 73J requires provides to comply with registration conditions. It is a condition of
   registration that providers comply with the Rules. The National Disability Insurance Scheme
   (Provider Registration and Practice Standards) Rules 2018 (the Practice Standards Rules)
   section 7(1) requires providers to be registered to provide Specialist Disability
   Accommodation (SDA). The provider is clearly advertising the provision of supports that you
   are not registered to supply.

3. The allegations and information held by the Commission indicate a significant amount of
   false claims against the Scheme, that could have otherwise have been directed to fund
   essential supports and services to people with disability.

4. The Provider’s practice of billing multiple NDIS participants for supports and services not
   provided compromised the integrity of the Scheme and deprived these NDIS participants of
   receiving necessary supports and services that they relied upon and were entitled to receive.

5. The information available to the Commission regarding the way in which the Provider
   handles complaints also suggests that the Provider has failed its obligation under the NDIS
   Practice Standards to implement a complaints management and resolution system that
   ensures that complaints made by all parties are welcomed, acknowledged, respected and
   well-managed. My preliminary view, based on the information available to the Commission,
   is that Provider does not provide a supportive environment for any person who makes
   complaints.

6. The matters set out above demonstrates conduct that falls well below the standard and
   quality of care expected from NDIS providers when providing supports or services to people
   with disability.

7. The information before me in relation to the protracted length of time over which this
   alleged conduct took place and continued as well as the instances of similar misconduct
   against multiple NDIS participants suggests that Provider’s conduct was systemic in nature.

8. My preliminary view is that the need to protect the interests of people with disability, who
   may be particularly vulnerable, and ensure they are kept safe, outweighs the Provider’s
   interest in remaining registered in these circumstances. I am also of the view that allowing
   the Provider to remain registered in the circumstances would jeopardise public trust in the
   Scheme.

9. Having considered the functions of the Commissioner, the objects of the NDIS Act, and the
   need to consider the financial sustainability of the NDIS in exercising the Commissioner’s
   powers under the NDIS Act, I consider that the registration of the Provider should be
   suspended under section 73N(1)(a) of the NDIS Act.




                              NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                              6
                                           1422
                                                                                                           T77
In deciding whether to suspend Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd registration, I have had regard to the
following matters as required by section 73N(4) of the NDIS Act:

a) With regards to the nature, significance and persistence of any contravention, or proposed
   contravention, of the NDIS Act (section 73N(4)(a))

       •   The conduct of Forward Focused Group towards NDIS participants is very serious and
           warrants action to ensure Forward Focused Group cannot continue to operate as a
           registered NDIS provider.
       •   The evidence available to the Commission strongly suggests that the provider is
           committing fraud by charging participants for services not provided, or excessive
           amounts. Based on information available to the Commission, it is highly likely that both
           Directors of Forward Focused Group (Ms Vida Reid and Mr Simon Reid) and the Chief
           Financial Officer (Mr Rejaul Alam) have committed the alleged fraudulent activities.
       •   Information held by the Commission also indicates that Forward Focused is providing
           supports and services that they are not registered to provide.
       •   The information provided by complainants also strongly indicate a pattern of bullying,
           harassment and intimidating behaviour displayed by the Founding Executive Director Ms
           Reid towards NDIS participants.


b) With regards to the action that can be taken to address any contravention, or proposed
   contravention (section 73N(4)(b)):

       •   Given the nature of the conduct described above and noting that it appears to be
           intentional and recurrent, the Commission considers it unlikely that the key personnel of
           Forward Focused Group will fully implement any corrective action prescribed by the
           Commission to address the provider’s contraventions.


c) With regards to the extent (if any) to which the person is conducting its affairs as a registered
   NDIS provider in a way that may cause harm to, or jeopardise, public trust in the NDIS (section
   73N(4)(c)):

       •   Based on the seriousness of Forward Focused and Vida Reid’s conduct and the potential
           impacts on NDIS participants, the Commission considers that there remains a significant
           risk to participants if Forward Focused Group was to continue providing supports to
           participants.


d) With regards to the health, safety or wellbeing of people with disability receiving supports or
   services from the person (section 73N(4)(d)):

       •   Forward Focused breaches of the NDIS Code of Conduct are particularly concerning. For
           the reasons detailed above, the Commission remains of the view there is an ongoing need
           to protect the interests, safety and wellbeing of vulnerable persons receiving disability
           supports and services.


e) There are no other circumstances considered relevant at this time (section 73N(4)(e)).




                                  NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                               7
                                               1423
                                                                                                         T77
Having regard to all of the matters set out above, I am satisfied that Forward Focus Group Pty Ltd
has contravened, is contravening, or is proposing to contravene, the NDIS Act (section 73N(1)(a)).

Taking into account the totality of the circumstances and the regulatory functions of the
Commissioner I have determined that it is reasonable and proportionate to suspend the registration
for a period of thirty (30) days under section 73N(1)(a) of the NDIS Act.

Opportunity to make submissions about a proposed revocation of registration under section
73P(4) of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth)


I am a delegate of the Commissioner for the NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission
(the Commissioner).

Proposed revocation of registration and banning order

Section 73P of the National Disability Insurance Scheme Act 2013 (Cth) (NDIS Act) gives me, as the
Commissioner’s delegate, the power to revoke the registration of a person as a registered NDIS
provider on the grounds listed in section 73P(1) of the NDIS Act. Relevantly, in relation to this
matter, I can revoke the registration of Forward Focused Group Pty Ltd ACN 643 878 639 (“the
Provider”) if I am satisfied that it has contravened, is contravening, or is proposing to contravene the
NDIS Act (as provided for by section 73P(1)(a) of the NDIS Act).

A banning order, which can prohibit or restrict specified activities by an NDIS provider, if the
Commissioner has revoked the registration of the person as a registered NDIS provider (as provided
for by section 73ZN(1)(a) of the NDIS Act.

Opportunity to make submissions

Before deciding to revoke the registration of a registered NDIS provider, the Commissioner (or a
delegate of the Commissioner) must give the person an opportunity to make submissions on the
matter, in accordance with section 73P(4) of the NDIS Act. A separate submission process in relation
to any proposed banning order made under section 73ZN(1)(a) is not required as set out in section
73ZN(8)(b) of the NDIS Act.

The purpose of this letter is to inform the Provider of relevant facts and the matters that I have
considered in reaching the view the Provider has contravened, is contravening, or is likely to
contravene the NDIS Act and to give it the opportunity to make a submission about this before I
make a final decision.




                                    NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission                             1
                                                 1425
                                                                                                           T78

I have also formed the preliminary view that the Provider should be banned from providing NDIS-
funded supports or services to people with disability in the event that I decide to revoke the
Provider’s registration.

I will not make a final decision about whether to revoke the Provider’s registration as a registered
NDIS provider until the Provider has had an opportunity to make submissions to me. This gives the
Provider an opportunity to tell me anything that you, as a representative of the Provider, believe
may be appropriate to bring to my attention, to dispute any of the facts of this matter, to comment
on the seriousness of it or to put your view as to decision I propose to make. You may also wish to
make comment on the banning order I am proposing.

Relevant facts and information

As a result of information provided to the Commission and the Commission’s own enquiries,
I understand the following:

    1. Forward Focused Group is a registered NDIS provider, registration id 4-4GHG-1073, trading
       as ‘Forward Focused’ (ABN 98 643 878 639).

    2. Forward Focused Group is registered to provide the following services:

                Item 8 – Assistance with travel/transport arrangements; and
                Item 20 – Household tasks.

    3. It is alleged that Forward Focused Group is providing supports to participants that the
       provider is not registered to provide. The FFG website (www.forwardfocusedgroup.com.au)
       in its ‘Service Offerings’ offers SDA (Specialist Disability Accommodation) at three suburb
       locations. The Forward Focus Group Facebook page posted on at least two occasions 18 July
       2022 and 28 September 2022 with the SDA service offering.

    4. Since September 2021, the Commission has received over 30 complaints regarding the
       safety and quality of supports provided by Forward Focused Group. The Commission also
       holds information that suggests that Forward Focused Group does not support individuals to
       raise any complaints they may have directly with the provider, without fear of retaliation
       from Forward Focused Group or the key personnel.

    5. This information strongly indicates that Forward Focused Group does not have a complaints
       management and resolution system in place that ensures that complaints are welcomed,
       acknowledged, respected and well-managed.

    6. The Commission holds information that Forward Focused Group does not employ workers
       who hold the relevant qualifications for their roles. The FFG website
       (www.forwardfocusedgroup.com.au) in its ‘Our Team’ section states that Ms Sally See was
       employed by Forward Focused Group as a Counsellor. Ms See does not hold qualifications
       with either the Australian Counselling Association (www.theaca.net.au) or with the
       Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (www.ahpra.gov.au). The Commission does
       hold any records of contact information or worker screening conducted for Ms See.

    7. The Commission holds information that the Provider is not acting with respect for individual
       rights to freedom of expression, self-determination and decision-making in accordance with
       applicable laws and conventions. Across June and July 2022, participants including Corina
       Abraham, Sarah-Jane Clulow, and Alexsis Bott all sort to amend or cease service agreements

   with the Provider. The written email engagement with the Provider indicated non-
   compliance with the National Disability Insurance Scheme (Code of Conduct) Rules 2018 and
   included both veiled and direct threats, bullying and harassment. By way of example,

       a. Across May and June 2022, the Provider attempted to obtain control of participant
          funds and participants supports for participant Alexsis Bott. When the participant
          confirmed, in writing that they didn’t want to take the action to release their funds

       b. Series of emails 24 June 2022 to 19 June 2022 regarding participant Sarah-Jane

          contract with us.”

       d. Series of emails 15 June 2022 to 19 June 2022 regarding participant Corina Abraham
          ceasing some services with Hybrid Hive. The participant seeks to meet to discuss

       f.   Email 16 June 2022 by the Founding Director to participant, Ms Abraham, “I would
            like all of your outstanding invoices paid immediately please or I will report this to
            the NDIS”.

NDIS Provider Register

Section 73ZS of the NDIS Act requires the Commissioner to maintain the NDIS Provider Register
which must include certain information for each person who is a registered NDIS provider. Relevant
to this matter, section 73ZS(5)(e) permits the NDIS Provider Register to include information about a
former NDIS provider, including information about the revocation of a person’s registration.

Should I proceed to determine to revoke the Provider’s registration and make a banning order,
information about the revocation and banning order will be included on the NDIS Provider Register,
available on the Commission’s website.

Making a submission

I have not made a final decision in respect of this matter and I will not until the Provider has had an
opportunity to make submissions in writing to me. This gives the Provider the opportunity to tell me
anything it believes may be appropriate to bring to my attention, to dispute any of the facts of this
matter or to comment on the seriousness of it.

Section 73P(4)(b) of the NDIS Act provides that the Provider may make submissions within 28 days
after receiving this notice. If no submissions are made within that time period, any revocation may
take effect as early as 7 days after the end of the 28 day-period. The Provider will be notified in
writing of any decision made in relation to the proposed revocation.

Any submissions the Provider may wish to make must be received by the Commission within 28 days
of its receipt of this notice unless it seeks, and is granted, an extension.
